what_it_does: RowHammer is a well-known hardware vulnerability in modern memory chips (DRAM — dynamic random-access memory, the main working memory in most computers): repeatedly reading from the same row of memory cells can cause bit flips in adjacent rows, corrupting data or enabling privilege escalation. The memory industry added a countermeasure in the DDR5 memory standard called Per Row Activation Counting (PRAC), which counts how many times each row is accessed and, when a row is accessed suspiciously often, issues a command to refresh the neighboring rows. This paper points out that the timing of those refresh commands is observable from outside: a row that has been accessed frequently takes slightly longer to respond because the memory controller pauses to issue a protective refresh, and this timing difference leaks information. The authors demonstrate PRACLeak, an attack that exploits these timing variations to extract a secret cryptographic key from a program running AES encryption, by timing memory accesses and correlating the slight delays with guesses about the secret. They then propose a defense called TPRAC that replaces the suspicious-activity-triggered refreshes with refreshes issued on a fixed, regular schedule regardless of access patterns, removing the timing correlation entirely.
